ai: A standard top-down merge sort needs O(n) extra memory. The merge step can't safely be done in place: as you pick the smallest element from the two sorted halves, you need somewhere to put it without overwriting elements you haven't read yet. That's the "second shelf" in the lecture, which is why merge sort needs about twice as much space. You allocate a temporary array of size up to n (a single reusable buffer, or temporary arrays at each merge, which are never larger than n at one time). The recursion also uses O(log n) stack space, because the depth is log n, but that is dominated by the O(n) buffer. So the total auxiliary space is O(n). This is the trade-off for the faster O(n log n) time, compared with bubble or selection sort, which sort in place with O(1) extra space but take O(n²) time.

ai: A standard top-down merge sort needs O(n) extra memory. Merging two sorted halves can't be done safely in place, so you copy the elements into a temporary buffer (the 'second shelf' in the lecture) while you step through both halves and pick the smaller element each time. At the top level that buffer holds all n elements. The buffers from the lower levels are smaller and are freed or reused after each merge, so they never add up. At most about n elements of temporary storage are in use at once, and a single buffer allocated up front can be reused across all merges. The recursion adds only O(log n) stack space, because the depth is log n. That is small next to the buffer, so the total is O(n). This is the trade-off against bubble and selection sort, which sort in place with O(1) extra space but take O(n²) time.

ai: The base case is n == 1 (or, to be safer, n <= 1), and it returns 1 immediately without calling factorial again. Mathematically 1! = 1 (and 0! = 1 too, so using n <= 1 handles 0 and avoids infinite recursion on bad input). The recursive case is return n * factorial(n - 1), which hands the function a smaller problem each call. As in the Mario pyramid, the base case is a question with an immediate answer, and each recursive call shrinks the input toward it, so the calls bottom out and the results multiply back up: factorial(4) = 4 * 3 * 2 * 1. Without a base case, clang would warn that all paths call themselves, and the function would never stop.
